This minimal difference occurred despite a 17% rise in gas prices between January and April 2024, a seasonal trend also observed in previous years. <2> The American Automobile Association (AAA) projected that a record 38.4 million people would travel by car over the 2024 Memorial Day weekend, the highest number for the holiday since tracking began in 2000. [1, 4, 5, 7] This figure represents a 4% increase compared to 2023 and a 1.9% increase over pre-pandemic levels in 2019. [1, 4, 5, 7] This was part of a broader forecast of 43.8 million total travelers for the holiday period. [1, 2, 3, 4] The projection signaled a very busy summer travel season ahead, exceeding pre-pandemic volumes. [1, 2, 3] <3> For the first time since February 2024, the U.S. national average price of gasoline saw a weekly decline, falling 1.9 cents to $3.63 per gallon as of April 29, 2024. This decrease was attributed to U.S. refiners increasing fuel output as they returned from spring maintenance. At the time, the national average was 8.4 cents higher than a month prior but 4.3 cents lower than the same time the previous year. States with the highest average prices included California ($5.35), Hawaii ($4.79), and Washington ($4.64), while the lowest were found in Mississippi ($3.03), Oklahoma ($3.06), and Colorado ($3.07). <4> As of March 21, 2024, the national average for a gallon of regular gasoline increased by 11 cents to $3.52. This rise in pump prices was primarily driven by the increasing cost of oil, which occurred despite lackluster domestic demand for gasoline. [3] This rise was primarily attributed to increasing crude oil prices, with the cost per barrel approaching $80, and a surge in gasoline demand as warmer weather approached. [2] Data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA) showed that gas demand grew significantly from 8.47 to 9.01 million barrels per day in the last week of February. All regions of the United States experienced a rise in pump prices. <6> In mid-February 2024, U.S. gasoline prices were rising for the first time since late 2023, with the national average reaching $3.27 per gallon as of February 18, 2024. A primary driver for this increase was the rising cost of crude oil. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude had increased by nearly 10 percent since the beginning of the year, trading at approximately $77 a barrel. <7> The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) released its February 2024 Short-Term Energy Outlook, detailing the impact of mid-January's cold weather on energy production. The report noted that the cold snap caused disruptions, leading to a decrease in U.S. dry natural gas production and a fall in crude oil output to 12.6 million barrels per day in January, down from a record high in December. The EIA forecast that production would rebound in February. Furthermore, the outlook projected that ongoing production cuts by OPEC+ would result in global oil inventory withdrawals in February and March, consequently placing upward pressure on oil prices during the coming months. <8> On January 4, 2024, the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline was approximately $3.09. The report noted that more than half of all U.S. fuel stations were already selling gasoline for under $3 per gallon. Looking ahead, AAA predicted that the national average might also fall below the $3 mark by the end of the year.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On January 29, 2026, AAA reported that a major winter storm with sub-freezing temperatures disrupted U.S. crude production and refinery operations. These supply issues caused a brief spike at the pump, pushing the national average price for a gallon of regular gasoline upward to $2.87. <2> AAA reported that the U.S. national average gasoline price experienced a slight increase to $2.84 per gallon in mid-January. Despite this minor uptick, overall pump prices remained broadly suppressed. This trend is consistent with established historical seasonal patterns, primarily driven by the year's lowest consumer gasoline demand and the circulation of cheaper-to-produce winter fuel blends, which allow for higher Reid Vapor Pressure (RVP) and incorporate more inexpensive butane. <3> The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) published its January 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), projecting that U.S. retail gasoline prices will decrease to an average of just over $2.90 per gallon in 2026. This forecast represents a drop of nearly 20 cents per gallon compared to 2025 averages. <4> GasBuddy has released its 2026 Fuel Price Outlook, forecasting that the annual U.S. national average price of gasoline will fall to $2.97 per gallon. This marks the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 that the projected yearly average has dipped below the $3 threshold, signaling a fourth consecutive year of declining prices and offering meaningful relief for household budgets. <5> Michigan implemented a major restructuring of its state gasoline tax system, completely eliminating the 6% state sales tax on fuel and raising the flat excise gas tax from 31 cents to 52.4 cents per gallon. This change, part of a nearly $2 billion transportation funding package signed by Governor Gretchen Whitmer, ensures that all fuel tax revenues are strictly dedicated to transportation infrastructure projects. <6> The Auto Club of Southern California reported that the statewide average for a gallon of regular gasoline in California dropped to $4.33, reaching its lowest price level of the year 2025 following a rapid pre-holiday descent. <7> On December 10, 2025, the American Automobile Association (AAA) released a forecast projecting that a record-high 122.4 million Americans would travel at least 50 miles from home during the year-end holiday period from December 20 to January 1. This represents a 2.2% increase over the previous record of 119.7 million travelers set in 2024. AAA largely attributed this surge in road trips to the national average gasoline price dropping significantly below $3.00 a gallon, making driving a highly cost-effective and convenient mode of transportation. <8> On December 1, 2025, the U.S. average retail price of regular gasoline fell below $3.00 per gallon to $2.98 per gallon. When adjusted for inflation, this marks the lowest average U.S. gasoline price since February 2021. <9> A retrospective analysis indicated that U.S. gasoline prices continued a downward trajectory in November 2025, with the average price for regular motor gasoline slipping to $3.05 per gallon. This represented a 0.3% decrease from October 2025 and a 0.1% drop from November 2024. The overall price decline was primarily driven by the seasonal switch to cheaper winter-blend fuels, lower seasonal travel, soft consumer demand, and sustained softness in crude oil benchmarks.
